classification.difficultyReason: Combines absolute-value inequalities with non-negative radicands, denominator exclusions and sign cases.

answer.short:
$x<-2$ or $x>2$.

The numerator is positive, so the denominator must be positive.
answer.worked:
A real square root requires a non-negative radicand, and $|x|\ne2$ because the denominator cannot be zero. Since $|x|+2>0$, the denominator must be positive:
$$\begin{align*}|x|-2&>0\\|x|&>2.\end{align*}$$
The domain is $x<-2$ or $x>2$.

answer.short:
$x<-2$ or $-1\le x\le1$ or $x>2$.

Require a non-negative radicand and exclude $x=\pm2$.
answer.worked:
Require a non-negative radicand and exclude $|x|=2$.

When $|x|<2$, the denominator is negative, so the numerator must be non-positive:
$$\begin{align*}|x|-1&\le0\\|x|&\le1.\end{align*}$$
This gives $-1\le x\le1$.

When $|x|>2$, both numerator and denominator are positive. This gives $x<-2$ or $x>2$.

The domain is $x<-2$ or $-1\le x\le1$ or $x>2$.
